outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no new resolution of the Oberwolfach problem for all orders has appeared; the one in-window event on the undirected problem is Meszka's 2024 complete set of solutions for orders 61 to 100, while the 2024 to 2026 preprints found concern directed or honeymoon variants, and no AI system is credited with any result on the undirected problem in any source I found.
problem_asks: (1) For every n and every 2-regular graph F on n vertices, decide whether the complete graph K_n on those same n vertices decomposes into edge-disjoint copies of F; the claim is universal over all n and all F. (2) The statement asks which 2-regular graphs have this property, so it asks for the class itself, equivalently for each n the set of F that fail. (3) For even n the literal wording (K_n on the same number of vertices) cannot hold, because K_n has odd degree n-1 and cannot be split into 2-factors; the usual variant removes a perfect matching, written K_n - I. The statement does not say whether that variant is intended, so both readings are recorded here and in the events.

events.what_happened: Mariusz Meszka, 'Solutions to the Oberwolfach problem for orders up to 100', Australasian Journal of Combinatorics 89(2) (2024), pp. 243-248. Abstract, read on the journal's HTML page: 'A complete set of solutions for all instances of the Oberwolfach problem for orders 61 <= n <= 100 is presented.' The journal PDF was unreadable through my fetch tool, so the solution tables and the method were not checked; a search summary describes a modified Bose-type difference construction, which I did not confirm.
events.revisions: No arXiv preprint or earlier version found. The AJC listing shows received 2023-05-13 (from a search summary, not checked on the page). The first public written version may predate 26 January 2024; the 2024 date is only the earliest public appearance I could verify, so the first-public date is not established.
events.delivers: Per the abstract, complete solutions for every instance of the Oberwolfach problem with 61 <= n <= 100. The abstract does not say whether the even-order K_n - I variant is included. A finite range of orders only: no claim for any n above 100 and no claim that the universal statement holds.
events.remains: Every order above 100 (this paper gives no bound), the universal statement over all n, and the even-order reading if the paper treats only odd K_n (not checked).

events.what_happened: A. C. Burgess, P. H. Danziger, A. Lacaze-Masmonteil, 'A complete solution to the directed Oberwolfach problem of order 2 (mod 4) with cycles of even lengths', arXiv:2602.16888. Per the fetched introduction, Theorem 1.5 says that for a bipartite directed 2-factor F of order n = 2 (mod 4) there is a solution to OP*(F) if and only if F is not [6]. The same introduction states that the undirected Oberwolfach problem 'has been completely solved for orders n <= 100', with exactly four 2-factors having no solution ([3^2], [3^4], [4,5], [3^2,5]), and that it 'remains wide open in general'. Those status statements are background to this paper, not its result.
events.revisions: v1 only (18 Feb 2026), 32 pages, 25 figures, no journal reference on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: A complete answer for the directed version OP*(F): directed 2-factors whose cycles are all of even length, on complete symmetric digraphs of order n = 2 (mod 4), with the single exception F = [6]. Nothing about the undirected problem, which the paper treats only as its starting point.
events.remains: The undirected Oberwolfach problem entirely, as the paper itself says; and the directed problem outside the stated class (other residues of n, and 2-factors with odd cycles, not checked).
events.direction: Cuts toward existence for the directed class it covers, with one stated exception F = [6]. It is a directed analogue, so it does not decide the undirected statement.
events.object: No counterexample. The result is a construction showing that OP*(F) has a solution for each bipartite directed 2-factor F of order n = 2 (mod 4) other than [6]. I did not read the construction, so I cannot say whether it is explicit.

events.what_happened: Daniel Horsley and Alice Lacaze-Masmonteil, 'Completing the solution of the directed Oberwolfach problem with two tables', arXiv:2408.10448. Abstract: the complete symmetric digraph decomposes into spanning subdigraphs each made of two vertex-disjoint directed cycles of lengths t1 (4 or 6) and t2 (even) with t1 + t2 >= 14. Combined with Kadri and Sajna, this completes the directed two-table case of unequal lengths, per the authors.
events.revisions: v1 only on arXiv. An Electronic Journal of Combinatorics publication (vol. 33, issue 1, 2026) appears in a search summary; I did not open it.
events.delivers: The directed two-table Oberwolfach case with unequal table lengths, in the authors' stated completion together with Kadri and Sajna. Directed only.
events.remains: The undirected problem, and directed problems with more than two tables.
events.direction: Cuts toward existence in the directed two-table case; a directed analogue, so it leaves the undirected statement untouched.

events.what_happened: Marie Rose Jerade and Mateja Sajna, 'The Honeymoon Oberwolfach Problem: small cases', arXiv:2407.00204. Extends the honeymoon result for n <= 9 to all cases with n <= 20 by computer search, per the abstract. The honeymoon problem seats n couples at tables of sizes 2m_i over 2n-2 meals; it was introduced by Lepine and Sajna in 2019.
events.revisions: v1 only; no journal reference on the arXiv page.
events.delivers: Honeymoon variant HOP(2m_1, ..., 2m_t) for n <= 20, by computer. Different question: spouses must sit together, which is not in the Oberwolfach statement.
events.remains: The Oberwolfach problem entirely; the honeymoon conjecture for n > 20.
events.direction: Honeymoon variant, so it is not a result on the Oberwolfach problem. Recorded as a discounted neighbour.

events.what_happened: Donald Knuth's note 'Claude's Cycles' (Stanford site, cs.stanford.edu/~knuth/papers/claude-cycles.pdf), announced around 28 February 2026, concerns decomposing the arcs of a digraph on m^3 vertices (each vertex with three outgoing arcs) into three directed Hamiltonian cycles. The PDF was unreadable to my fetch tool. A secondary article (implicator.ai, 8 Mar 2026) reports that Claude Opus 4.6 found a construction for odd m, GPT-5.3-codex and GPT-5.4 Pro handled even m, and that Kim Morrison formalised the proof in Lean on 4 March 2026. None of this is quoted from the authors' own text.

summary: The Oberwolfach problem (Ringel, 1967) is settled for all sufficiently large n by Glock, Joos, Kim, Kuhn and Osthus (arXiv v1 12 June 2018; JEMS 2021), with Keevash and Staden giving an independent large-n route (arXiv April 2020). Small orders were handled by computation: Salassa et al. up to 60 (arXiv 2019, AJC 2021) and Meszka for 61 to 100 (AJC 2024). The 2026 Burgess, Danziger and Lacaze-Masmonteil preprint states that the undirected problem is completely solved for n <= 100, cites Deza et al., Meszka and Salassa et al. for that, and says the problem 'remains wide open in general'. The only in-window event on the undirected problem I found is Meszka's 2024 paper. Its date is not pinned: the AJC listing gives receipt on 13 May 2023 (from a search summary), and I found no preprint, so the first public appearance I can verify is the 2024 volume. Whether it counts as a 2024 event therefore turns on that receipt date. The in-window preprints I opened (Santizo Huerta and Keranen, Feb 2024; Jerade and Sajna, June 2024; Horsley and Lacaze-Masmonteil, Aug 2024; Burgess et al., Feb 2026; Akbari, Mar and Jul 2026) concern Hamilton-Waterloo, honeymoon and directed variants and are recorded as discounted. Wikipedia's status text was read through a summarising fetch of the live page, which is a 2026 revision rather than the January 2024 frozen text. It names the four exceptions OP(3^2), OP(3^4), OP(4,5) and OP(3,3,5), says that 'it is widely believed that all other instances have a solution', and says GJKKO gives all but finitely many instances; I could not check that wording against the frozen revision. The 2026 introduction agrees on the four exceptions. The gap that matters most: GJKKO's abstract gives 'all large n' with no explicit threshold, and I found no source that explicitly covers orders from 101 up to that threshold. Whether the even-order K_n - I variant is covered by GJKKO or Keevash-Staden is also unresolved, because I did not read their bodies. On AI: no AI system is credited with any result on the undirected problem in any source I found; every OP event I read is computational, difference-method, or non-constructive, with no AI named. The Knuth 'Claude's Cycles' note (Feb to Mar 2026) credits Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5.3-codex and GPT-5.4 Pro, per a secondary article, but it concerns a digraph Hamiltonian-cycle decomposition, not K_n into 2-factors, so it is recorded as a neighbour with ai.none_found false and no systems entered, because I had no authors' own sentence to quote. The OpenAI Astra roundup (Aug 2026) lists ten results with none on this problem; the OpenAI primary page returned 403 and I relied on a news summary. Close calls: (a) Meszka's census of finitely many orders may move nothing under section 2.1, since it leaves the universal claim open; I recorded it as an event with its scope limited to 61 to 100. (b) The frozen wording for even n is ambiguous, since K_n with n even cannot decompose into 2-factors, so I recorded both readings. (c) The GJKKO threshold is not explicit in its abstract, so whether orders 101 up to it are covered is open on what I read.
competing_reading: On the strict section 2.1 reading, Meszka's finite census of a universal claim moves nothing, so the problem has no in-window event and its status rests on GJKKO (2018/2021), Keevash-Staden (2020) and the pre-2024 computations. On a looser reading, Meszka extends the verified range from 60 to 100, and the 2026 statement that the problem is 'completely solved for n <= 100' records a status that a later pass may count as movement. The second reading also needs the date of Meszka's first public write-up, which I could not establish.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The January 2024 frozen Wikipedia text for this problem, to test the status claims against the frozen state rather than the live page. (2) A readable copy of Meszka's paper, for whether its solutions cover the even-order K_n - I variant and whether any non-existing cases occur in 61 to 100. (3) The body of GJKKO, for an explicit threshold on n and whether it covers K_n - I; this decides whether orders 101 up to the threshold are settled. (4) Meszka's first public version or a receipt-to-publication record, to fix whether his write-up predates 26 January 2024. (5) The body of Keevash and Staden, for whether the even-order variant is covered. (6) An arXiv full-text search for 'Oberwolfach' with AI terms (AlphaEvolve, language model, Lean, GPT, Claude) for 2024 to 2026, to close the AI search, which I ran only through a general web index.
